utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Now we are going to resume our proceedings and if I am not mistaken, we are going to resume with yesterday's witness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour, yes. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Osmancevic. Please be seated. Now we are going to pursue with your testimony. Now, I would remind you that yesterday you made a solemn declaration whereby you would speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Are you going to go on in the same vein this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please answer the questions from the Prosecutor's Office, if you would. DZIDO OSMANCEVIC (continued) Examined by MR. NIEMANN (continued)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmancevic, yesterday, just before we broke up in the evening, you were telling us that you had been taken to various places for trench digging and you mentioned places such as Loncari, Kacuni, Kula, and so forth. I wonder if you would look at the map that I now show you, please. If this map could be put on the overhead projector and I will give you a highlighting pen. Perhaps it could first be marked as an exhibit, the next in order for the prosecution. (Handed). Show it to Mr. Mikulicic on your way through, please, if you would. Now, looking at it on that particular -- on the video projector there, with that highlighting pen, would you be so kind, if you can, to mark some of the places that you recall that you were taken to for the purposes of trench digging? Could you mark them for us. When you mark them, tell us which ones you are marking, if you would, for us, just say the name of the place when you mark it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kula.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you put a heavy mark on that, so we can see it, that is the idea.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that is a good one. The next one? The next place that you went to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kula, Loncari, Bare. I cannot remember the other parts. I mentioned some of them yesterday. I have forgotten -- I cannot find my way on a map so well, but I will try.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, if you would. Take your time, there is no hurry. If you look up and see Bare, can you see Bare there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try. Yes, Kudanic, Nadioci, that region. I found Bare. I know this area, Jazvine, I did not dig there, but I did dig between Rona and Bare. Round about here. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you put a circle round about here. What about on the other side of the river, is there any towns up there you were taken to dig, what about Loncari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try and find Loncari, on the other side. Loncari and Komari, I dug there too, in Komari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see Komari there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can see them. I had a field of my own there but I just passed through there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is near where you had your own property, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A little lower down. That is I dug below my own field, my own property.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. I will tender that, your Honour, if I may. Now, Mr. Osmancevic, you said when you first went to the camp you stayed in the hangar of the camp and it was when you were in the hangar that you were taken out in order to do digging. Can you describe for us, as best you can, the circumstances? What it was like when you went digging these trenches; what were the conditions like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning when we would start off for the trenches, we were not allowed to look around too much, we had to get straight into the truck. Maybe I told you all this before, maybe not. There was this table with the registrar, he would take note of our names and surnames, then we would enter the truck. I remember the driver very well, Padovani, and his order was not to look left or right but just to enter the truck, to be taken to our destination, our digging destination, all the points I mentioned. When we came to the place we were to dig, he said: "If somebody escapes, I kill the rest", that is what the guard would say. Food was brought to us every 48 hours. On the first 20 days it was very difficult, the Red Cross would bring us food. I am not quite sure when the Red Cross arrived with the food. Yes, I do remember the divisions and Kula -- Podjele and Kula, we dug a great deal without being given food or water. Perhaps I am speaking a little fast, I can slow down if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could go just a little bit slower it would make it easier for the interpreters, thank you. You were about to tell us of the conditions that you had to work under. For example, how long did you have to work, not every day but what was the sort of longest period you had to work without a break; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were no pauses, you were not allowed to have a break or we tried to do this ourselves, but I did not have a watch with me. About 48 hours or more, that is what the others told me too, but I was not able to look at my watch and see exactly how long it was, but about 48 hours or more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you feel, at any time in danger of being shot from people from the other side of the line, the front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning, like all of us, we thought we would be there for two or three days, five days at the most. But, when I went digging for the first time, in the swampland I lost all hope of getting away from there ever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see soldiers on the other side that were firing in your direction at any stage when you were out trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was difficult to see any soldiers. I am speaking of myself, my own experience. I did not see any soldiers, I could not see them. This was -- you mean the Bosnian Herzegovina Army, but whether there was ammunition -- yes, we could hear rifle fire but high up near Podjele, whereas a journalist from the Croatian side, when two of our fellows were wounded in Bare, the army was not able to shoot there. The journalist, himself, saw this. There is a particular spot where -- well, I will tell you of that event too, because it is in the centre, along the centre, the prisoners were wounded, the detainees were wounded. In front of them there was a soldier and behind them there was a soldier and there was not any shooting there, in front and behind. They asked us about this. Some said it was the army, some said it was not. I personally have my own supposition; some of the prisoners said yes, it was, and they cursed when the journalist arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were kept in the hangar for a while. Then what happened after being kept in the hangar; were you moved somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in front of the second hangar with the cells, which is where the warden was and probably the other guards who slept there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know, or come to know, who the warden of the camp was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned who the warden was during the first three days. He said: "I am your warden. If anybody needs a doctor or anything else"; we did not think we would stay there for very long. Now, how far he was able to influence any of these matters, I do not know, but we lost hope after several trench digging experiences. Then he worked in Zenica as well. I do not know what he was there in the prison, but somebody told us that he was a policeman, a militia man and that he knew his brother-in-law and he called him on the phone. We did hope that we would be released, but afterwards we lost all hope. From the very beginning I know that we were dealing with Zlatko Aleksovski, we were told this name by the man who worked with his brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him on the occasions before or after you had been taken out for trench digging; this is Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we went trench digging, in the instances that I went trench digging, and when our names were written down to go digging, I myself never saw the warden. I never saw him present when our names were taken down. Ljubo was there. I called him Pisar, his nickname is Pisar. Whether he is a guard or whether he has a higher office, I do not know. They did not wear any insignia, maybe they did have some insignia, but I did not know of it. The second was Zec, but the warden in my presence when I went trench digging and while I was in the camp, I never saw him. When we come back can -- came back from the trenches he was present, not every time, but on occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he do. What did you see him do when you came back from trench digging on those occasions that he was there? When he was there, what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually at the entrance to the second hangar with the cells. He was outside the hangar. When it got warmer he was on the other side and would be sitting on a bench in front of a fire. When we were returned on several occasions, he would ask us whether we are all there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would he ask you or would he ask one of the guards whether you were all there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually he would ask who brought us with -- he would talk to Mr. Ljubo, not with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubo, I think, was the gentleman who took your names down originally; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there ever an occasion when people were, in fact, missing when you came back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In my presence, while I was digging in Bare, I am quite sure that three people went missing, maybe four. I am not quite certain, but I, myself, can vouch for three, because they were close to me, I was up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of these people that went missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They live in close by villages, near Loncari. Sunula Pasic, Rasima Salih and the third is, his name is Ramo, he is from Loncari too, and he was wounded, and a young man was in one of the convoys, whether he was a driver or co-driver, he was from Tuzla. He was a Hodza. Whether he actually was a Hodza or not, I am not sure. Whether his surname was Hodza or his nickname was Hodza, but the drivers used to refer to him as "Hodza", "the Hodza". He was wounded there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when these three went missing, when you returned to the camp? What did Mr. Aleksovski do in relation to these three that were missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what he did, but when we returned, and there was a lot of torture that day, both with regard to wounds, wounding and they would line us up to shoot us and they did not, but when we came back Aleksovski would ask, I do not know whether exactly he asked Ljubo or Padovani, I think Ljubo was there too. He would have in his hand his list with our names and he would ask: "Are they all there?" Ljubo would just hug Aleksovski and walk off with him towards the hangar. He put his arm round him and I could not hear what he said to him. I do not know what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, the person that had the list when you returned was Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if he had his own list, but Ljubo quite definitely did have the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Aleksovski with a list; whether it be his own or anybody else's does not matter, did you ever see him with a list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how often did you see him in the camp, Mr. Aleksovski, in the whole time you were there? Did you see him only once or twice or did you see him on a number of occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On a number of occasions. I saw him throughout my time at the camp, either when we returned or when we left for the trenches. Several times, particularly in the summer time when the days got warmer and he was outside more often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him more often when you were in the cells as opposed to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever, on any occasions, have a conversation with Mr. Aleksovski, while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On how many occasions, can you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when it was that you had this conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was when I was transferred to the second hangar, about a month -- 20 days or a month later. I do not know exactly when I was transferred, but Aleksovski did not come to the door, the guard came to the door and took me to the place where he lived and we talked there about the problems; shall I carry on and tell you about that or not?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You might tell us firstly where it was as precisely as you can, that you were taken to. You said, "the place where he lived". Where was that in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was at the entrance to the second camp, right by the door. I do not know exactly whether it was on the left or the right; left-hand side or right-hand side, but it was on the entrance. He had his office there, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have described that as, "the camp". Is that where the cells were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, where the cells are. That is where I talked to him for the first time. We were already in the cells. That was about a month later, 20 days after I had been taken there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell us, what did he say to you and what did you say to him, as best you can recall? What was the nature of the meeting that you had with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guard was present, the guard who came to take me to call me to the telephone because one of my neighbours had been taken prisoner with the BiH army and he told me that my mother was a witness for that neighbour, that he had committed some crimes, and that I was to telephone. They gave me a number in Zenica and to talk to my mother. But, as my mother is a diabetic, I was not able to talk to her. My sister came to the phone and Aleksovski was present during that telephone conversation, along with the guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you to make the phone call; the guard or Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aleksovski told me, because he had already called another prisoner, who worked with his brother-in-law. He also called him to come. He stood by the telephone and one of the receivers was held by Aleksovski, the other was held by me. The telephone had two receivers. I said: "Yes, were you a witness? You should withdraw your testimony." That is what I said. But she did not go to testify against this neighbour, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that you should tell your mother to withdraw her testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To withdraw her testimony, the guard told me this. I do not know whether he did too, but I know that -- I remember that he said to the guard: "Well, Stipe until the neighbour comes out, we are not going to let him out either, Stipe will come."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Until the neighbour goes out, we are not going to let him go either"; tell us who you mean by that. "Until the neighbour goes out", what does that mean; until the person was released in Zenica, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Zenica they meant Vinko Vidovic by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until he was released, you were not going to be released, is that what you meant, by that you said there? Until the neighbour goes out --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, your release was to be dependent upon the release of this person in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. Although I did go out although Vidovic was still there. He was released later on. That is what I heard, or maybe he did not leave by that time, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was Vinko Vidovic being held, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere in Zenica. I do not know, I did not pay any visit to him because it was not possible to go there, to visit people there, and I had problems of my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an understanding that he was being held in custody or was he free, or what did you understand when you made this phone call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding was that he was in detention, since he had been captured as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you had made this phone call and spoke to your sister, what happened then? What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, he told me that I should not talk too much over the telephone, so I just, you know, said that I was okay and I told her to tell the mother to withdraw the complaint. Then she said that she did not even do that, that she did not even lodge a complaint. So, Aleksovski just nodded his head. He stopped -- he cut me off and that is basically what happened until Vidovic is released. After that I was left alone, they no longer called me about that. I was returned to the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the only time that you ever had a conversation with Mr. Aleksovski that you can remember, or was there any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you that I used to see him, but that was the only conversation that I had with the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned in your evidence how you were taken to the cells. Yesterday, you marked on Exhibit P18 the place -- the hangar that you first went to. If the witness could be given P18 again, please. I would like you to mark with the highlighter the letter "B", the location of the cells, if you can remember, in Kaonik camp that you were taken to, that is the second location. (Handed). If you could put a big "B" for me at the spot where you think the cells are that you were taken to subsequently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you look at the photograph that I now show you? Perhaps that might be marked the next exhibit number in order. Could you please show it to Mr. Mikulicic before you show it to the witness? Perhaps you might return the exhibits on the ELMO to the Registrar, please. (Handed). Your Honour, I am not sure that I actually tendered Exhibit P18. If I have not done, I now tender that, it having been marked on the two occasions. Just looking in that photograph that is now appearing on the screen, do you recognise that at all? It is not a terribly good photo but you may be able to recognise it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can recognise the photograph. I can see the table at which we used to sit and eat. I do not remember the number of the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to mark approximately, to the best of your ability, where your cell was, the cell that you were put in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might put the letter "A" there for me, so we can be sure that is where it was. The windows into the cells themselves, where are they? Can you indicate those from that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not know exactly about the others, but this is one of them. (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us mark it with the letter "X". I wonder if you could do something else for me. Could you draw an arrow pointing in the direction of where Mr. Aleksovski's office was. Draw an arrow. I know it probably is not shown there but if you draw an arrow in that direction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Fine. I tender that, your Honours. The arrow is very faint, but it is at the bottom. Perhaps if you show the witness that one too, please. (Handed). The next photograph, might that be marked the next exhibit number in order, please? I tender the photograph that was just marked by the witness. Mr. Osmancevic, did you know where any of the other prisoners in the camp were kept, in the cells were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Across my cell there was some drivers whom I did not know very well, but in the big -- in the large hangar there were some people I knew. Down there, as we used to sit at the table, because we used to eat together, people would come out from other cells. There was a man -- two men from Karina region, a Croat and a Muslim. They ate with us and they were also exchanged with us, but the Croat was kept by them. The two of them I think were members of the army and that is how they were captured. Down there, down the corridor, there was a Croatian soldier whom I never saw. I only heard him scream as he was being beaten. And there was another one who used to eat with us. I think he was an Arab, and there was a man by the name of Hando from Han Bijela, who also used to eat with us. He was in one of the cells down there. I do not know exactly which cell exactly they were kept. Anyhow, they were in the lower part of the corridor. Across my cell, there were those drivers and my neighbours and here, this Croat must have been because we used to hear him -- we used to hear noise coming from that direction. (Indicating). Here, on the other side, I am not sure whether the Arab was there or whether it was Hando who was kept there. Anyway, the two of them were kept here, in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, you must just for me do the following, where you think the Croat was kept, you might put a "C". Just write the letter "C", where you think he was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where you think the driver was kept you might put the letter "D".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where you think the Arab person was kept you might put the letter "A" for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is E, it appears as E there. Thank you. I tender that, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor's Exhibit 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, I ask that we go into private session. It is just a matter of turning the sound off outside, if I could, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. (Private Session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Osmancevic, were you then subsequently registered with the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you became registered by the ICRC did circumstances in the camp change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did, quite a bit. After wed were registered by the ICRC and given blankets we did not remain the hangars for very long. The situation was somewhat better. It really meant a lot for us when the situation was quiet at the front-line because whenever there were problems at the front-line, we had problems as well. When there was fighting going on in the battlefield, we would be taken out to dig trenches and if one of their soldiers was killed, there would be retaliation and so on. As long as the situation was quiet, we were left alone as well. After the ICRC registered us, I was transferred to the other hangar, next to the warden's office. The food was much better there. It is true there were people coming from the field, soldiers who would enter the cells. They used to beat people, abuse us verbally, and so on, but you could say that the situation improved after we had been registered by the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you then exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After two months and six days, I was exchanged, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What date was that; do you remember -- the date of your exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was on the 19th June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think, your Honour, I have tendered all the exhibits that I have shown to the witness. If there is any of them which have not formally been tendered I do so now. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, considering the fact that the witness was talking about an event which has been unknown to the Defence until now -- namely, the telephone conversation in the office of the accused -- I would kindly ask the court to enable me to have some consultations with my client. I would like to have a short break, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I just might say, firstly we have no objection, if your Honours are disposed to give Mr. Mikulicic a break, we do not object to that. I would like to indicate on the record that we did indicate to Mr. Mikulicic that this conversation that he now refers to was something we learned of when the witness came to The Hague just very recently to testify, that was the first we heard of it. We wrote to Mr. Mikulicic and told him there was a conversation, so it is not quite as though he has never heard of it before, but certainly he has not heard of the details of it and it was not in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees, and we are going to have a recess. I think three minutes, would that be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the interpreter understood that rightly, whether it was three or another figure?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you say "three minutes", your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 30 minutes is what his Honour said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. (9.53 am) (A short break) (10.25 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We shall now resume our proceedings. Mr. Mikulicic, please proceed. Cross-examined by MR. MIKULICIC

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Mr. Osmancevic, my name is Mr. Goran Mikulicic. I am the Defence counsel of Mr. Aleksovski. I am going to ask you several questions. Would you please answer them to the best of your ability. Mr. Osmancevic, before the conflict in the Lasva Valley, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jelinak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that village in some way divided? Are there several parts of the village or is it a exact whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a exact whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I wrong if I say that there is the upper and lower part of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One part -- I do not know how to explain it to you -- one part has an upper and lower part, upper and lower part of the village, but in the upper part, there are no Croats. In the lower half, I, myself, have a neighbour who is a Croat. He is my neighbour, and all this lower half is for the most part a mixed population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was to have been my second question. Let me repeat: what is the national composition -- what was the national composition of the village of Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in percentages?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not in percentages, I am sure you do not know that. Was that exclusively a Muslim village or were there some other nationalities living in Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not exclusively Muslim. The Serbs lived a little apart, but all of us were there, Croats and Muslims in Jelinak proper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmancevic, you said that you had a Croat as a neighbour. Can you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vidovic Vinko, Ivo Brnada, Plavcic Zilan, Brnada Niko, Brnada Slavko and several others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was one of the neighbours perhaps Mr. Stipe Andrijasevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was at the cross-roads a little further off from me, about 500 metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you knew him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We went to the brigades together. We worked together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmancevic, where did you go to school and what school did you finish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to school in Zenica to the metallurgic school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before that to the primary school in Kaonik. In fact, eight forms of primary school and four classes in Putis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it regular schooling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmancevic, did you serve in the JNA Army before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Sabac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you commissioned in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Awarded a commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your introduction that in 1992 you were a member of the Patriotic League; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let us get things clear. I do not know if you are mixing things, by Territorial Defence, Patriotic League, and whatever. The Patriotic League, the real army perhaps existed, but in the village, in the villages, as I told you earlier on, the Territorial Defence, we were altogether. Whether it existed later on before the conflicts or after the conflicts as the Patriotic League, I do not recall. But I know that we were all in this TO, Territorial Defence, before the army was formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I am asking you this so that you can explain to me whether, during the events in the spring of 1993, whether you were a civilian or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in civilian clothing, just like my other neighbours, Croats, but they were in uniforms and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking you, were you a civilian or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I am a soldier -- if I were a soldier I would have been ready from top to toe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were a civilian, is that my correct deduction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Osmancevic, were you a member of any political party at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not a member of any party, but I did vote for my own side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is your own personal affair, I am not asking you that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just wanted to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Osmancevic, was there any fighting around your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What fighting, if Stipe Andrijasevic's son guaranteed security and safety and a little bit of armaments, but it was mostly hunting, weapons and as they were together in the militia at the time, when the HDZ took over the leadership, they were in the militia until we had to give up all our weapons and they said they guaranteed our safety, and you can see what kind of safety they guaranteed in the long run.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not quite sure that I have understood the answer to my question: was there any fighting around the village of Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no fighting at all. While we were in the village and when we were taken from the village there was not any fighting but afterwards there was. Some went to dig trenches but I did not have to go to dig trenches, they did not ask me to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmancevic, do you recall the day when you were brought to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, who brought you to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was -- brought by imprisonment, or who transported me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that my neighbour, Plavcic Mirko drove the van, the blue van, he is also a neighbour, he lives near Stipe, he was the driver. The co-driver was from Setulija, another village. I know him from my school days, but I cannot recall his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this transport van secured in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw no security upon entrance into the van because if someone guarantees your safety, then they will not put a sock over your head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took you in when you came to Kaonik, did anybody take you in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that particular day, nobody, on that night. Who took us in? The guards of the camp, Cakic Anto and some others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said guards. Who were the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that they were in uniform and that they had an insignia, an emblem of the Croatian Defence Council, HVO. The insignia had the letters "HVO".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you differentiate between the guards and the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot. They all had the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you mentioned yesterday the defenders of the homeland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some elderly people in front of the prison, the home guard, and they brought some of the people -- cigarettes to some of the people they knew, people whom they had worked with or were neighbours with. There were two of three of them, and one was a Serb. As I said, if he was in camouflage, then he had civilian trousers. If he had camouflage trousers he would have a civilian jacket or vice versa. But these were only older people. Those who were there all the time and who were younger, they were in uniforms like the warden all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was their function when -- you mentioned these elderly people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not enter into the hangars, they were in front of the hangars. I just saw them as ordinary guards. When we were let out in those first few days, we had no lavatory. When we were transferred to the other hangar we did have a lavatory, but when we would go out to dispose of the -- to empty the empty the buckets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These home guards, did they have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some old 48s from the JNA Army, some old rifles. They did not have any automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, if I understood you correctly, at the time when you were brought to Kaonik, there were two types of guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It would appear so; some older guards and some younger guards. They would say that they were the home guard. They would call themselves the home guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know, did some of the guards go to the front-lines, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us something more about that? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know that because Dzemo Medugorac, a good guard, he was from Medugorac, he said Dzemo went to the front-line or somebody else would be said to come back to the front-line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they went up to the front-line, who looked after the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were not only two guards. There were the ones -- the bullies who beat us. I told you who the real guards were. They were the guards and the real guards, there were few of us in the camp, so we did not need many guards to guard us. Mr. Ljubo and the warden took shifts. There was always somebody there. They were the guards, whereas the bullies were others. Those who did not go up to the front-line. If somebody did not want to go to the front-line so he, himself, was beaten. My friends used to tell me that he had, in fact, not wanted to go up to the front-line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who beat him, I do not understand? Who was beaten by whom? Did you see this, did you witness this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, no, but I heard the screams, cries, the noise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not going to ask you more about that because you saw nothing yourself. Tell me, Mr. Osmancevic, you have described the fact that one of the detainees, one of the prisoners, was Semsudin Kovac and that he escaped. Do you know what the circumstances of his escape were? Did you see anything yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said I did not work with him and I did not see why he escaped or where he escaped to, just like none of the others saw this. Nobody saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know whether, during your stay in Kaonik whether there were any other escapes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the ones who went digging, he escaped but he returned. That was during the attack. There was an attack while we were trench digging and I saw him wearing civilian clothes later on when I left Loncari. He went off with a pickaxe and everybody wanted to escape from the grenades. That is that particular person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of any other escapes apart from Semsudin Kovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here in the camp, no; from the camp, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "here in the camp, no", did you hear of any other escapes elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I take into account the other prisoners, then there was always a lot of talk about who disappeared, who was wounded, who was killed, and so on. But I did not pay attention to those stories much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmancevic, do you perhaps know that some of the prisoners in some other way left Kaonik or was released from Kaonik in some other way? Apart from escape or exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember. Perhaps -- but if I remember later on, I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about the conditions prevailing in Kaonik and the food, in particular. What kind of food did the guards eat? What food did they get? Do you know what food the guards were given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When we were transferred to the second hangar with the cells, the food was better there. I think that the guards ate the same food. They did not eat together with us, but we were told they were given the same food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the conditions in the prison. Mr. Osmancevic, can you tell me please: during your stay in Kaonik, did you notice or see the existence of anything? I have in mind covers, heating, blankets, heating or any kind of facilities which you were lacking in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the first hangar. We did not have any of this in the first hangar, but when we were transferred to the second hangar we did have blankets. The food was better, as I already said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you did. I just wanted to tell you, was there anything that you saw that existed but you were not given -- you did not have access to, when you went to the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I dug a lot without any pause and on the last day, when we were to be exchanged, we were taken to Kula to be exchanged. As far as food and blankets are concerned, we did have food and blankets. As far as any rest was concerned, during our digging, we did not have any rest. We had to dig trenches for 48 hours or more. No water or food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Kula. Do you perhaps know who the commander at Kula was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Loncari. Can you describe to us who took you to Loncari, if you know who did? Who took you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was Padovani with the truck. There were vans as well. The van, whether they took me to Kratine, Loncari, and who the driver was I am afraid, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I might remember later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmancevic, let us go back to the telephone conversation that you described earlier on in the office of the warden. Who came to fetch you, to take you to the office for that telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stipe Andrijasevic, my neighbour came to fetch me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He is your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you describe for us, please, in connection with that telephone conversation, what the role of Vinko Vidovic was? He was also your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Well Vidovic's role is the following: When I was brought by Stipe Andrijasevic, who came to the camp, to my cell, to fetch me, he said: "Come out for a moment".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In as much detail as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came, Stipe, to my cell. He said: "Would you come out?". He called out my name and surname. Even if I did not want to, I had to. I came out of the cell. He took me to the office where there was a telephone and the warden was there and Vidovic -- Vinko's father was there. I knew him. He was an older man. I think Stipe's younger son was there too. He asked me -- Stipe: "Do you know why you have been brought here?" I said: "No". "Do you know that Vina has been taken prisoner?" "No", I said. "Do you know that your mother is a witness -- Vina is being tried in Zenica and your mother is a witness?". "No, I have no idea. How would I be able to know? You know that I am in the camp and how I was brought here". Then, the agreement -- then we had this agreement whereby we would remember somebody and remember the telephone number. I said: "You know that I have nobody in Zenica; nobody has a telephone in their flats". "Try to remember", they said. Then I remembered Miro Hadzic had a sister in Zenica. I went to him, to fetch him and he gave me the telephone number. He was taken back to his cell. Then I phoned this number and asked him to call my mother to come to the phone. Stipe Andrijasevic wanted my mother to withdraw her testimony, because Vidovic Vinko said that she was one of the witnesses in that case. I called Amidzic's sister and this is what happened tomorrow. I asked them -- I said I would ring them the next day. I did ring them the following day again and I did not talk to my mother, but I talked to my sister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your sister's name? It is Fatima, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I asked my sister whether what they said about my mother was true. The warden had one of the receivers by his ear. I was told not to talk too much, not to say that I was in prison but to say I was alive and well, to talk about Vina in that particular case, to withdraw my mother's testimony. My sister said she was never a witness, she never went and none of these other things that they were saying -- and the warden looked at Stipe and I shrugged my shoulders and said: "There you are, my mother is not a witness". Then the warden cut off this telephone line -- the telephone line. Stipe said: "Does your mother know that you are in our hands?" The warden then said: "We are not going to release him until Vina is released, that is what it boils down to". I stood around in the office for sometime. Vina's father did not say a word during all that time. He just cried because he was sorry for his son. Was I clear enough?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you were clear enough. Let me just ask you several more questions: while you were waiting for the telephone connection, did you have anything to drink, perhaps? Were you given coffee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I had nothing to drink.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Osmancevic, what you have just described to us in this entire event over the telephone conversation, if I have understood you correctly, and please correct me if I have not, your neighbours were included, Stipe, Vina Vidovic. They are all people who you know previously. Am I correct in saying that they asked you to do them a service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would appear that way. But what service could I do? My sister told them my mother was a diabetic, that she could not leave her house --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry for interrupting you, so your mother did not supply them with any testimony, any statements. So it was a misunderstanding, in fact, if I have understood correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, misunderstanding, but I understood something, that I was being asked to do something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Osmancevic, you said that on the 19th June you left Kaonik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think it was the 19th June. I have a ticket --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, the date is that not important. What I want to ask you is something else. Do you know what happened with Vinko, when was he released and was he ever released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was accused -- condemned of something -- I do not know. I was not able to follow the case, but I think he was exchanged later on. When and how I do not quite know, but I do know that people said he was exchanged somewhere around Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this exactly, before or after you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after your release?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not quite know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether his release and your release coincided? Did it have any relationship -- was it linked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmancevic, are you personally -- were you beaten ever in Kaonik personally? Did anybody hit you in Kaonik ever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me and two other people were never beaten. This was just luck. It depended on luck whether you were beaten or not beaten. But unfortunately, I did -- my luck ran out when I dug trenches. I had to dig trenches all the time but I was never beaten. I was lucky there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No more questions, your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecutor's Office, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Witness, in your examination-in-chief, you used the expression "the Hodza", what do you mean by "the Hodza"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hodza, that is how they called him. Whether Hodza was his last name or whether he was a Hodza, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Osmancevic, you are now done with your testimony here before the International Criminal Tribunal. We would like to thank you most heartily for having come to this Tribunal. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Counsellor, would you like to bring in the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I call the next witness for the prosecution, I would wish to make an application similar to the one I made yesterday in respect of the witness. His name -- the next witness's name is contained in the inventory which was filed before your Honours' court dated 16th February. It is in an inventory of witness statements and the name appears at number 4 on that list. In respect of that witness, your Honours, I am seeking permission of your Honour's court to have protective measures in place, moving your Honour's Chamber so that pseudonym "B" -- that the witness be assigned a pseudonym, and the letter "B" be assigned to the witness and he also be granted face as well as voice distortion in his testimony. Your Honours, I have indicated this to my learned friend, learned counsel for the Defence, and I understand that he has no objections to my application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees, and would ask that the appropriate measures be taken. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning. Please stand. Thank you for having come here this morning. You are now going to read out the solemn declaration which the usher is going to be presenting you with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please be seated. Now, you are going to answer the questions which the counsel for the Prosecutor's Office is going to be putting to you. (11.00 am) Please proceed. WITNESS B Examined by MR. MEDDEGODA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you -- witness, I am giving you a sheet of paper now. Could you look at the sheet of paper and confirm whether the name which appears on that sheet is your name or not? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be shown to learned counsel for the Defence. I am tendering, your Honours, that sheet of paper containing the name of the witness as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your religion is Islam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Maybe we could adjust the witness's microphone. Please see to that, usher. Can you hear me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Can the interpreters hear as well? I think we can pursue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember 25th January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, do you recall where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at home in Busovaca, my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise for interruption, we do not hear anything, my client or myself. We cannot hear the voice of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Could the technicians make the appropriate arrangements? Is it possible to get this working? Just one minute, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I can hear the interpreters, I can hear the Prosecutor and I can hear the court, the judges, but I cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So the problem is that Mr. Mikulicic can hear everyone, except for the witness. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Can we continue? Has everything be settled? Mr. Aleksovski, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSOVSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can hear you very well, but in order to listen to the witness I have to take off my earphones, I think it is a bit complicated but other than that it is okay. I do not know, I will try to listen to the witness now that he starts speaking and see if I can hear very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Well, maybe the technicians would want us to have a recess so they can get all this working properly. So I have not been given an answer; 10 minutes to get this worked out. Right, I do apologise, Witness B, but we are going to have a recess for technical reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Before the recess, can I have redaction of line 2 on page 44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Now, we are going to have a 10-minute recess to get these technical problems straightened out. (11.11 am) (A short break) (11.27 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think we should be able to resume now. So counsel for the Prosecution, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, you said you recall 25th January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Busovaca, in Ravanjska road, in the neighbourhood of Ravanjska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you alone on Ravans --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were you alone in the neighbourhood of Ravanjska Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that morning, I went to have coffee to my neighbour's house, together with three other neighbours and we did not finish the coffee and members of the HVO, round 6.00 am, opened fire and started firing at us. The house started burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do when the house started burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We put out the curtains and couch and we hid under the stairway. The members of the HVO kept shooting all day long and we simply could not leave the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that there were members of the HVO who were shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could tell by their uniforms and HVO insignia and also because they held the power in Busovaca and they had something against us, simply because we were Muslims and the area where we lived was a Muslim area. There were only Muslim houses in that area, that is why they were shooting at us. Later on I was taken prisoner by them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the uniform that is worn by the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore camouflage uniforms. Some of them were wearing civilian clothing but most of them had HVO insignia with Croat chequer boards on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did this firing last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout the day, the whole day, until 5.00 pm when they started approaching our houses and when we surrendered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Together, you too surrendered to the HVO forces on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And together with you, did others surrender as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my neighbours surrendered as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many others surrendered together with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three more persons who surrendered apart from myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- did you happen to know any of the HVO soldiers who came to your village -- who came to that settlement that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know the Pusic brothers, Smoljo -- brothers, they were all my neighbours from Busovaca from the Busovaca Valley area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you and the other three surrendered, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then the HVO soldiers started mistreating us. I had to walk around barefooted and they also forced me to go to the house of my neighbour and one of the brothers of the HVO soldiers forced me to go there -- forced me to break into his house and he was shooting around and he said: "Look here, this is all a Croatian area, only one population only, one ethnic community should be living in this area", and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were forced to break into a house of one of your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. I was forced by an HVO member to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when you -- did you force yourself into that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He fired the rifle all around the house. He had a Kalashnikov, he just broke into the house and he fired a burst of gunfire all across the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, what did you have to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, they collected us, there was a commander here and they wanted to shoot us, they wanted to execute us, but then one person came -- I think he was a commander -- and he started cursing at them, "let these people go". Then this commander -- I suppose he was a commander -- we had to raise our hands like this, put them behind our necks, and we were taken to the Kaonik camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you taken to the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my neighbourhood we went to the bus stop. They made us walk with our hands behind our necks and Zeljo Bubreg, the driver from the Zenica Trans company, took us in his bus to the camp. JUDGE NIETO NAVIA: I am sorry, but I do not know whether it is necessary to switch off and on the microphone every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I thought that when the witness answers-- it is so sensitive that his voice might. JUDGE NIETO NAVIA: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Do you know what the Kaonik camp was prior to the war. I think I have got to switch it off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not a camp, it was a former JNA barracks; I know that because I used to pass by when I went to Zenica by bus. We used to pass by Kaonik. On the right-hand side there is this Lektif cafe. Here the cafe, there was the entrance to the JNA barracks. The HVO had a plan about that. They wanted to destroy the Muslim population and they set up a camp there and organised the cells and everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what time was it when you arrived at Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the evening. It was between 5.00 and 6.00 pm on that same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the camp, at what point did you have to get off the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they took us in, the bus started out from the main road and then there is a 100 metre long dirt road and we had to walk to one of the hangars with our hands behind our necks. We were forced to do that by the HVO members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am tendering an aerial map of the Kaonik camp, which I would be pleased if the usher could show to the witness. There are copies for the court as well as for learned counsel for the Defence. That document, your Honours, may be marked as Prosecution Exhibit P22 -- P23, your Honours. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be P23, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you place the photograph on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where do you want me to point?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, please, point out the place at which you got off the bus when you reached Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a second. There is this road here. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You may take your time with that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Please show on the photograph on the ELMO, on the projector. If you point it out on the photograph on the projector. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the main road leading to Zenica, and this is the turn that you have to take to go to the Kaonik camp. These are the hangars. (Indicating). This is the one were I was brought to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before getting to the point were you were brought to, can you tell this court the point at which you had to get off the bus when you reached Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at some point here, on the road -- on the way from the barracks to the hangars. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then when you got off, you said you had to walk a distance to your hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had to put our hands like this. (Indicating). They brought us here in front of this hangar here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had to have your hands behind your neck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To this one here. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please circle that building and mark that with letter "A"? If you use the marker and circle that building and mark it with the letter "A".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were taken to the hangar, could you tell this court what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that evening, when I was brought there, there were about two or maybe even 300 Muslims there. The HVO members kept bringing in more Muslims to the hangar and there were only wooden pallets in that hangar and maybe a blanket that was supposed to be shared by two persons in that hangar. On the same evening -- maybe around 2.00 or 3.00 am -- members of the HVO arrived, including Mr. Aleksovski, and they came to make a list of us. I know him, I can recognise him. He introduced himself as the prison warden. He said he was the warden of that prison. He said -- he told us his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, could you, please, look around in this court and say whether Mr. Aleksovski, the person who introduced himself as the warden of the prison, is present in this Trial Chamber today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There he is. That is the gentleman in question. (Indicating the defendant).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Perhaps it should be made clear in the transcript that the witness pointed towards Mr. Aleksovski. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said that HVO members at that time made a list of the persons who were brought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe to this court how the list was made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they brought some candles and some military torch lights. There was a table there. We were standing in a line and they put down our names as we would approach the table, each of us. In the meantime some of the people were returned during that night. People who were over 60 or who were severely sick, they were returned to their homes by the HVO soldiers during that night. But those who were taken back on that night were later on returned to the camp again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also registered that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would submit that, at this stage, your Honours be pleased to move into private session for a few questions and answers that I would wish to go down on the record which otherwise would reveal the identity of the witness. For that reason, I would submit that your Honours, we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Fine. We will move into a private session then. (In private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. After the registration in the camp, where were you put into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In camp A, that is where we were that night. On the pallets we had to crouch down, two sharing a blanket in that hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where your other neighbours were put into that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night I said -- as I said -- when I came there were about 300 and the second morning there were about 500 Muslims in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anything happen to you the next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next morning my name was called out. I cannot say which of the guards called out my name. A member of the HVO took me to the settlement where I lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who took you to the settlement where you lived; do you know the names of those HVO guards who took you to the settlement where you lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Ivcan Rajkovic and Niko Grubesic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you were taken to that settlement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Members of the HVO took me to that settlement. When we got there we had a rifle from the settlement -- a Romanian rifle for the settlement, which I gave them. It was with a neighbour in a chicken coop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave that rifle to the HVO soldiers who took you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, were you brought back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. That is right, they took me back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were brought back to the camp, were you returned to the same building that you had spent the previous night, or were you returned to a different building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took me back to the same building. On that day, 20 or 30 of us were called out by name. There was a roll call for 20 or 30 of us from hangar A. They took us to this other hangar, where there were 16 cells. I think Mr. Aleksovski ought to know this, 16 original prison cells here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were taken out of that building, which is marked as, "hangar A", and taken to a different building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, please, point out on the map that you have on the projector to which building you were taken on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Building B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How many of you were taken to building B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 20 or 30 of us group were taken and sent to cells. I was taken to cell number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Together with you, were others put into cell number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 16 cells. Most of us that were called out were taken to cell number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any others who were put into cell number 6, together with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would submit that my next question and answer would be moved into private session, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Fine, we are now in private session. (In private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, could you describe the interior of cell number 6, to which you were put into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The cell was located on the right-hand corner next to the lavatory on the other side of the hangar, on the far side of the hangar. The cell had two small windows, 40 by 60 centimetres on the outer side. It had the entrance door, a wall and bars, iron bars above the door. The cell was, looking at it in length, it was about 50 to 60 centimetres long and two metres wide and it had wooden boards where we sat and slept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that cell, did you have heating facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were two stoves in the corridor, but then one of the stoves was taken away and there was one in a hangar -- this hangar. (Indicating). The two stoves were divided between the two hangars and the stoves were in the corridors, not in the cells; no heating in the cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any electric lights in the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the cell, but in the corridor and so as there was the iron bars above the door, then there was a little light coming in through the iron bars into the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From inside the cell, could you observe what was happening outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could see what was happening in the corridor. There were roll calls and when members of the HVO would call out the name of a Muslim, for example. While the Muslim said which cell he was in, then you would hear beating and you would hear water being splashed across him to bring him to after the beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I would advise you not to be so fast in your answers so the interpreters will be able to translate your answers accurately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was taking the roll calls out in the corridors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Members of the HVO, the guards who were on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when the roll was called out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whoever was called out knew that he would get a beating. They called out the names of the people who had been taken to dig the trenches and to form human shields, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your name ever called out by HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. After seven to eight days spent in the cell my name was called out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when your name was called out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they called my name out, 19 other Muslims were called out by members of the HVO and we were taken by truck to the "11 Plavih" inn to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were taken by truck to 11 Plavih inn, by truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From there, where did you have to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From there, once again accompanied by the HVO guards. The 11 Plavih is the name of an inn. They took us to dig communication trenches at Prosje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender five excerpts of Exhibit P34 for the court, as well as learned counsel for the accused and the witness? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution's exhibit number 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, could you look at the exhibit on the ELMO and point out Prosje, where you were taken to dig trenches? Could you look at the projection on the projector? Prosje, that is the place where you were taken to that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mark that with the letter "A"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).
