utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe to this court what happened in Prosje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got to Prosje we were divided up by the HVO soldiers to our positions for trench digging and dug-outs and we dug the whole day until late at night, until about midnight. There was no maltreatment there, they were fair on that occasion, the members of the HVO who were with us, and about midnight, around midnight, they took us back to the inn, the 11 Plavih inn and we were taken back to the Kaonik camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the only occasion on which you were taken to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the next morning we, with a RAB, we were taken from Krcevine to Kula to dig trenches again the next morning. Petrovic was the driver of the RAB truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many detainees were taken on that day to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 20 of us. 20 of us. Myself and 20 others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please mark on the map that you have on the projector the place to which you were taken, the place in Kula to which you were taken for trench digging on that day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please mark it with the letter "B"? For how long did you have to dig trenches in Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We dug trenches that whole day and the whole night. In the morning they told us that representatives of the ICRC had come to see us, to verify us, and to take down our names as detainees in the Kaonik camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then were you brought back to the camp the next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We dug the whole day and the whole night. Then on that morning they took us back to the camp so that the Red Cross could make -- register our names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you went back to the camp that morning, did the Red Cross arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you registered by the members of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I have their identification card of the ICRC. I have an ID from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender a copy of the ID card of the Red Cross pertaining to this witness as Prosecution Exhibit 25. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think we are talking about a protected witness. I am not sure you want to identify the witness, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: It may be under seal so the identity of the witness is not revealed. It need not be put on the ELMO, your Honour. It may be shown to learned counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For how long did the registration process take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About -- it took us up to noon. By noon. They had finished by noon, and as soon as the Red Cross had left, the HVO read out our names again, did the name control, Krilic Marko was one of the HVO guards. The roll call was taken once again and we were sent back to Kula to continue digging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you have to continue digging in Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We dug a whole day, the whole night. Then they took us back to camp for the Red Cross visit. Then we were taken back that whole day and another night. So all in all it was two days and two nights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any mistreatment when you were digging trenches in Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was, by the members of the HVO. Three groups of 20 of us, 60 people were beaten up on that occasion. I was one of them. I took a serious beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe to this court what happened to you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the members of the HVO -- their nicknames were Hosovac, Maglajlija and Kakanjac and many other members of the HVO, some of them were masked with socks over their heads and faces. They started to call us out by name, one by one or two by two. They took us out and started hitting us, beating us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. That is exact. I was beaten amongst -- I was taken out amongst the first, one of the HVO members ordered me to open my mouth. When I opened my mouth, he cocked an automatic gun in my mouth. I managed somehow to move my head away and the gun went off round my shoulder, but none of the bullets hit me, I do not know how. The rifle fell from my mouth to my shoulder and went off, he fired it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything else happen to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He cursed me, he cursed my balija mother. Then he threw the rifle away. I do not know whether it was an automatic gun, a Kalashnikov, or what. He took a semi-automatic rifle with a bayonet, he cursed me and my balija mother again and he scratched me here. You can see the mark here, with the knife and across my nose. So across my neck and across my nose. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken out many more times after that. We dug trenches all the time and in the meantime the members of the HVO would take out from the line one or two people and beat them up seriously, gravely beat them up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you had to dig trenches after coming back from the camp, after the registration by the ICRC the whole day and the whole night; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was it when you finished digging the trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We dug trenches the whole day and the whole night. In the morning, as they had beaten up myself and my colleagues, four of us were beaten up. Then they saw that we were no longer able to dig. The next morning they took us back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you taken back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us back by truck. Myself and my three colleagues who were very gravely beaten. Us, the Muslims who were with us, through orders by the HVO guards, they carried us and threw us into the RAB truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came back to the camp, were you taken for any medical examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken along with two of my colleagues. I was taken by the members -- I do not know who they were -- in camouflage uniforms with the HVO insignia and they took us to the medical centre in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who requested that you be taken to the medical centre in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We asked to be taken to, but they saw the condition we were in, that we needed help, we could not get up. It was just a formality, a pure formality. The sisters there did not even touch me with a finger. It was a pure formality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and your other beaten colleagues requested that you be taken to the doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To which health centre were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to the health centre in Busovaca, near the petrol pump, where IFOR is stationed now, but it was always a health centre there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before me, my two colleagues were taken there, Lah Ahmed and Cakara, and Ibreljic Mustafa, who succumbed to his wounds. He was beaten up so badly that he died as the result. Me and my colleague were taken -- they told me to take off my clothes, to bare myself up to my waist, to bare my chest. They asked me who I was, what I was, and when I said I was born -- that I was -- they cursed my balija mother. When I said "helijode" instead of the Croat equivalent for 1,000, which is "tisoco", nobody wanted to look at me. They were nurses, female nurses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In short, you were not examined at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I -- I did bare my chest but nobody came up to me. I do not know if they even wrote my name down or gave me tablets or an injection, nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not treated for your wounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They did nothing, absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, were you brought back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long -- for how many days thereafter did you spend in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About three to five days because I did not want to dig any more trenches, I was returned to hangar A. I was taken back to hangar A to sleep on the pallets. There was over 100 of us there, 150/200 of us who had been beaten up. As we were unable to dig trenches any more, we were taken back to hangar A with the wooden pallets on the floors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said about three to five days later -- you said you spent about three to five days thereafter in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. After having been beaten up, and on the eighth or ninth day the International Red Cross came back and I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the exchange, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not taken. The ICRC members, when they came to verify us, I asked them whether there were any -- what rights we enjoyed as detainees, as prisoners. They said that there were three possibilities: one possibility was to remain in Busovaca, but that nobody on the side of the HVO could guarantee our safety there. The second possibility was to be taken to Zenica, the third to be taken to Kacuni under the control of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you hope to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the days that you spent in the camp, witness, did you have sufficient food to eat and water to drink and also water to wash yourselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were in the camp, we got two pieces of bread, very thin pieces of bread, a plate -- one plate for two prisoners. We had to eat from the same plate. It was very watery beans. The food either was not salty or very salty. As for water, we would knock on the door of the cell if we were thirsty. If the guard was good he would ask the HVO to bring us water; if not he would not, he would say: "What do you want water for?".

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: That is all, your Honour, in cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Prosecutor. Mr. Mikulicic, would you like to proceed with your cross-examination at this stage? Please proceed. Cross-examined by MR. MIKULICIC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Witness B, my name is Mr. Mikulicic, I am Defence counsel for the accused, Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski. I will ask you a couple of questions and I will ask you to give me an answer to these questions to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For about two or three years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean prior to the conflict before 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in the vicinity of Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know many people in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, because I worked in Busovaca. I also worked in Zenica, but I used to pass through Busovaca on my way to Zenica. This was my municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any problems with your health before? Did you have to see a doctor often, before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I can prove that. As for my health, thank God, it has been very good always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to the day when you were taken to Kaonik. You said that early in the morning HVO soldiers came to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no, it was not early in the morning. Early in the morning I went to my neighbour's house to have coffee with him and sirens were sounded around 6.00 am and members of the HVO opened fire on the Muslim neighbourhood from all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did HVO soldiers want from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What they wanted from me? Before the conflict, HVO soldiers had all power in the area and the area was decorated with chequer boards, the Busovaca was simply covered with them, and they kept telling us things, like us being Muslims, not being welcome there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe you have not understood me, Witness B. I wanted to know whether HVO soldiers wanted something from you, whether they wanted you to surrender something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who do you mean by "you"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me personally?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I mean you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wanted to know whether I kept anti-aircraft weapons, rocket launchers, things like that, but there is evidence to that. There is not a single house -- Muslim house -- were weapons were hidden, and you know very well which houses were burnt down and which were not during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you have any weapons, any weapons that you gave over to the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me personally, I did not have anything. In my street we had a rifle called Rumunka which I surrendered to them, but it was not my personal property. It was a rifle called Rumunka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: If I may interrupt my learned friend. I am moving for a redaction of a line which I have sent to the Registrar. Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Mikulicic may be shown the answer which needs to be redacted. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you surrendered to the HVO soldiers two hand grenades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two hand grenades, yes, that is correct, when they came to arrest me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, where did you get those hand grenades from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where I got them from? Well, I bought them before the fall of Jajce. I cannot tell you exactly who sold them to me, whether it was a Croat or Muslim. Anyway, I bought them in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us why, to what purpose, did you purchase them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question: why did you buy these two grenades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I bought them with my own money. You mean that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I do not mean how, I just want to know what did you intend to use them for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I wanted to use them for? I simply wanted to have them. It was war time. I cannot tell you what my intention was. In the name of Allah -- I do not know what to tell you. I just wanted to have them. That is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did HVO soldiers tell you when you surrendered these two hand grenades to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing. They just forced me to walk around barefooted. They forced me to break into my neighbours' houses, houses belonging to Smoljo and Pusic. I was forced to walk around and it was a January morning, a cold morning, I was forced to walk around barefooted. They would not let me put on anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you were a civilian or a soldier at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I was a civilian. If I had been a soldier -- and let me tell you there was not a single dug-out in our street, not a single trench. We did not even stand guard in our street. Of course I was a civilian, I was wearing a civilian clothing when I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that you were taken to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in chief that the Kaonik prison was set up by the HVO, according to a previously conceived plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it used to be a barracks. It is correct, just wait a second. It used to be a JNA barracks, that was this hangar A, where we were brought to, and the barracks was under the control of the HVO. Let me tell you, you know who built all those cells? Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not know, witness, that is why I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know because I was there. That is why I am telling you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when this construction work was performed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not long before that, because you could see that the paint was quite fresh on the walls. No, not long time before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know how long before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was not there at that time, but I can guarantee that it was not long before that. I used to pass by Kaonik and I knew what hangar A looked like as opposed to hangar B. You could tell that it was done for Muslims, for Muslims to be kept there and they used to say that openly. They used to say: "These cells are waiting for you, balijas".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that construction work being done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tell me, is there any barracks that you could really get close to and see for yourself what is happening? But the mortar was fresh, I am telling you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time do you exactly have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not more than a year before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that there were no hangers before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was this hangar. Only the cells were built later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true -- it is true, is it not, that you did not see for yourself when the cells were built?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct, I did not see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who brought you to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not brought there. They drove us there. It was Bubreg Zeljo in his bus that drove us there. There were also some HVO members who were escorting us and carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But who took you in at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who did what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took you in? Who spoke to you when you got to Kaonik? Did anyone speak to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They just told us to put our hands behind our necks and they brought us to the hangar and the doors were closed and nobody spoke to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Aleksovski from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I met him on that occasion, when those people came to verify us. He said that he was the warden of the prison and he said what his name was, Aleksovski. That is when I met him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did say something, but I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you remember exactly what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I do not know whether it was him or another HVO member that said that, you know, what I mentioned about those who were elderly or sick. I do not know whether it was him who spoke about them or one of his colleagues. Anyway, somebody said that those people would be returned to their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But some of them were, indeed, returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how it was established who was sick and who was not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some people had their medical documentation on them, like diabetes, heart condition, you know, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, those who were above -- over 60, those were released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that on the following day, the HVO soldiers took you back to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that you handed over a rifle to them on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they know about the existence of that rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they kept taking roll calls and one of my neighbours said that there was a rifle there. In the meantime, my name was also called and I was taken there and when they asked about the weapons, I gave them the rifle that we had over there in our street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you get the rifle from? Did you buy it as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not buy it, I cannot tell you that; I do not know: I do not know where it came from, its origin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from that gun, did anybody from your neighbourhood turn over any arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not from my neighbourhood, no. The members of the HVO know this. I do not remember, no. Nobody did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken to the mahala alone or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anybody was taken. I cannot say exactly. They took me and others. The guards kept calling out names. The people who were taken away were brought back, beaten up and others taken and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not know whether anybody else laid down his arms from the mahala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that only you had two grenades and a rifle?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Witness B, you said that you were taken out from Kaonik to the terrain to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took you from Kaonik to the terrain, to the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards in the camp who read the roll call.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who accompanied you to the digging site? Were you accompanied, escorted by the guards from Kaonik or by some other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once I was taken to Prosje, twice -- I cannot say exactly. They put us into the truck. Whether they were these guards or others, I do not know, but they were members of the HVO. Whether it was guards or some other escorts I cannot say, because when you are in the truck you put your hands behind your back and we are told to lie down, so I could not really see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the digging site, were you watched over by anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were members of the HVO, there were the lines there. Members of the HVO, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you watched over by the same guards who were in Kaonik or some other individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some other individuals. Some other members of the HVO. They were not guards from the Kaonik camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the events when you were harmed, injured, and you said that, at your request, you and some others were taken to the health centre at Busovaca, to a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any one of the medical staff in Busovaca health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beforehand, or when you were taken there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were taken there. Or before, prior to the event.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Previously I did know some of the staff. Dr Rozika Kordic. But on that occasion there were two female nurses or doctors, I do not really know, some others walked up the corridor. When I was there there were two females there. Whether they were nurses or doctors, I do not know, they did not say who they were. But I did not know them. They were unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn later on who these two women were, whether they were nurses or physicians or doctors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, how? Who would tell me that, when the health centre was in the hands of the HVO, how could I learn that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that after these events, you never returned to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I passed through Busovaca, but never -- no Muslims, sir, no Muslim ever, not only myself but no Muslims who were sent out of Busovaca ever returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us of the injuries you sustained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had two broken ribs here; I had a knife wound here and across my nose, knife sore and my nose was broken up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether your wounds were registered into a physicians' record? Was a record made of your wounds and injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where, in Busovaca, you mean, or in the part under the control of the army?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see them write anything. They just said -- no, I cannot say. I cannot guarantee one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you feel, health-wise, after the examination? Were you mobile, were you able to move?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was just able to move. Somebody had to lift me because for two months I was not able to get up. I had to be raised by some individuals. But once they managed to get me up, I was able to move around a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you seek medical aid later on when you had left Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in Zenica. And then they put some balms on me, made from honey. Some balms were placed on my wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did this for you? Who administered these honey balms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the hospital when I was in Zenica there were no tablets, no injections, no X-rays, there was no electricity, so some of the doctors, when they sent me home and then my wife administered these honeycomb balms on my wounds, because there were no medicines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the examination at the Busovaca health centre, were you sent out to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come you never went to dig the trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I had returned from the health centre, they took me back to hangar A and all those members of the HVO who were Muslims -- the Muslims who were there, nobody went back to work from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that you refused to do any more hard labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came -- some of the guards came to me from time to time and all those who were of a certain age were told to stand up. As I was not of that particular age, I was not taken. I said: "I cannot walk, sir", and there were no problems there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us earlier on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may interrupt my learned friend. I am moving, your Honours, for the redaction of lines 2 to 6 on page 75 of the proceedings and of line 1 on page 81 of the proceedings. These may be shown to my learned friend, your Honours. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please proceed, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, your Honours. Witness B, you told us earlier on that you were in cell number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was with you in cell number 6? You mentioned Emin Saracevic, Senad Ermercic and Novalic Edin; do you remember any other names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but it is not essential.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the court what their names are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not want to tell you their names. Why are those names so important to you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B, do you refuse to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not refuse to answer the question, but why are they important? I guarantee that Brizo, Senad Ermercic and Novalic were there. I cannot remember any more names. I do not refuse, no, I would gladly tell you, but I just cannot recall the other names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B, can you tell us whether, during the time you spent at Kaonik camp, there was another person of the same name and surname as yourself? Was there anybody else of that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Counsel for the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Well then, Witness B, you have concluded with your testimony. Thank you very much for having come before this Tribunal. Just one second, let us bring down the curtains. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, as regards the next witness as well, I am seeking measures for protection. Of course, in his case, I am only moving for a pseudonym to be assigned to him and that he be assigned the letter "C", as well as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Given the fact that we only have 15 minutes remaining, I think we should take due account of peoples' needs. Perhaps it would be best not to start now because we would be cutting off the witness in the middle. I do not know what you think, but I think we leave it there for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I am inclined to agree with your Honours. In that event, the witness could be summoned to court tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, can you go along with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. We agree, because really there is no point in examining the witness for about 15 minutes and then interrupting him. It is better to start tomorrow and hear the whole testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for your cooperation and for your understanding. We want to do things as expeditiously as possible, but there are other aspects that we do have to take into account as well. I think it is best for us to call it a day and then tomorrow we will be back. See you all tomorrow. (1.00 pm)
